defaults.permitted_development: Across Wiltshire, boundary walls, fences and gates are usually permitted development if they stay no higher than 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles and no higher than 2 metres elsewhere, or if an already-higher boundary is altered without increasing its height. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: Across Wiltshire, for ordinary houses, most fence and wall questions come back to the same split between the 1 metre highway-side limit and the 2 metre limit elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: Across Wiltshire, means of enclosure are not controlled by an extension-style depth formula. Height, siting and visual effect do the main planning work.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Wiltshire, front and corner boundaries often need more careful design than enclosed rear-garden boundaries.
rules.roof_rules: Across Wiltshire, ordinary boundary rules do not create a roof allowance. Gate canopies or covered entrance features should be checked separately.
rules.materials_rules: Across Wiltshire, material choice is usually a design issue rather than a standalone permitted-development test, although listed-building and conservation-area contexts can make inappropriate boundary finishes much harder to defend.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even modest boundary changes can need fuller scrutiny where an existing wall, railing or gate helps define the street scene.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building controls can apply to fences, gates and walls where they form part of the building's curtilage or historic setting.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions are a common reason why an otherwise modest boundary change still needs planning permission.

rules.permitted_development: The ordinary householder route for a fence, wall or gate usually depends on the height and its relationship to the road: 1 metre by a vehicular highway, 2 metres elsewhere. Listed-building settings and removed rights can change that answer quickly. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: For ordinary houses, most fence and wall questions come back to the same split between the 1 metre highway-side limit and the 2 metre limit elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: Means of enclosure are not controlled by an extension-style depth formula. Height, siting and visual effect do the main planning work.
rules.boundary_rules: The same boundary treatment can be acceptable in one position and need permission in another once it fronts a road or sits on a prominent corner.
rules.roof_rules: A simple gate or wall is one thing; a roofed gate feature can be quite another. Covered entrance elements should not be assumed to sit within the same fallback.
rules.materials_rules: There is no prescribed material palette for ordinary fences and walls, but prominent frontages are easiest to justify when the boundary treatment fits the surrounding street character.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status can tighten the position for boundary works, and separate consent may be needed to demolish an existing wall, fence or gate that contributes to the area's character.
restrictions.listed_building: Historic boundary walls and railings are often part of a listed building's significance, so replacement or removal can need listed building consent.
restrictions.article4_notes: A planning condition or Article 4 direction can override the standard boundary limits, so even a straightforward replacement fence may need consent.
